rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabbat is formally informative but can perform loss as a curse or as an enacted divine ruin; the curse also conveys blame and condemnation.
rows.anchor: tebâb oldu bu fiil esasen ihbâra mevzû‘olmakla beraber ibare

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many interpreters of the first revelation took the phrase as an imprecation, hence the common rendering “may his hands wither.”
rows.anchor: İlk nüzûle nazaran çokları bu mânaya haml eylemişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “May his hand wither” first suggests paralysis, but figuratively asks that he be bankrupt, powerless, and frustrated in every effort.
rows.anchor: “Eli kurusun” tâbiri daha ziyade شَلَّتْ يَدُهُ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “May he be ruined” or “ruined he was” better captures tabāb; Abu Lahab’s later confirmed ruin makes the declarative sense especially apt.
rows.anchor: Bunu “yuf olsun, yuha gitsin, berbat olsun” diye ifade etmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah’s placement after the Prophet’s victory and Abu Lahab’s death signals fulfilled foretelling: his ruin only deepened, while the wording still condemns him.
rows.anchor: bu sûrenin tertibde buraya konulması bunda ihbar mânası maksud olduğuna

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His two hands stand for every means he tried to use, for or against, in worldly and religious affairs; all his efforts against the Prophet and Islam turned against him.
rows.anchor: gerek müsbet gerek menfî, gerek tutmak gerek itmek için kullanmak istediği

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab is singled out between the surahs about the Prophet and God despite other unnamed enemies; this marks him out among the criminals, echoing Yasin.
rows.anchor: Ona وَٱمْتَٰزُوا۟ ٱلْيَوْمَ أَيُّهَا ٱلْمُجْرِمُونَ [Yâsin 36/59] mazmûnu üzere

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His special distinction is more lamentable because he was the Prophet’s paternal uncle yet opposed him; the contrast exalts the Prophet and divine truth above lineage.
rows.anchor: Çünkü Ebû Leheb Peygamber’in baba bir amcası olmak haysiyetiyle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The epithet “Abu Lahab,” literally father of flame, represents fire-spewing enemies of Islam, so his ruin exemplifies theirs and points to God completing His light.
rows.anchor: “Ebû Leheb” şahsı gösteren bir künye olmakla beraber lügaten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kunyas can denote a characteristic as well as a person’s name; Abu Lahab therefore alludes to being hell-bound without ceasing to refer to the historical man.
rows.anchor: kinayeler hakikatin iradesine mâni‘olmayacağına binâen burada bu mânanın ehemmiyet-i mahsûsası

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His given name was Abd al-Uzza; his red cheeks brought the fire-associated kunya, initially suggesting brightness, fiery temperament, or severity.
rows.anchor: Onun asıl ismi Abdüluzzâ b. Abdülmuttalib iken yanakları pek kırmızı olduğu için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kunya’s real implication became his conduct: by choosing hostility and refusing faith, he made himself a source and lover of fire, a model of hell’s people.
rows.anchor: bunun hakikatinde bir ateş kaynağı olmak veya ateşi sevmek mânası bulunduğu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite his kinship and status, he persisted in hostility; his fate should make other unrepentant enemies of the Prophet consider their own ruin.
rows.anchor: Peygamber’e buğzedip de tevbe etmeyen diğerlerinin ne kadar ebter ve bedbaht olacakları

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari gives three reasons for the honorific kunya: Abu Lahab was known by it, it avoids his name Abd al-Uzza, and it suits a person of the Fire.
rows.anchor: Keşşâf’ta der ki: “Tekniye tekrim ifade ederken burada künye ile anılmasında

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: One explanation is that Abu Lahab was simply famous by his kunya rather than by his personal name.
rows.anchor: Birisi ismiyle değil, künyesiyle şöhretidir

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: A second explanation is that the text avoids his personal name, Abd al-Uzza.
rows.anchor: ikincisi ismi Abdüluzzâ olduğu için ondan udûl olunmuştur

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: A third explanation is that the kunya suits him as one of the people of Hell; the pattern also names an evil person Abu al-Sharr.
rows.anchor: Üçüncüsü meâli نَارًۭا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍۢ olan ehl-i nârdan olduğu için künyesi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And he was ruined” separately states that Abu Lahab himself failed, missed his aim, and perished in loss.
rows.anchor: Evet, Ebû Leheb’in iki eli yuha, hüsrana gitti, tebâb oldu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab supported Quraysh financially at Badr but could not attend because of illness, sending As ibn Hisham, Abu Jahl’s brother, in his place.
rows.anchor: hastalığından dolayı Bedir’e bizzat iştirak edememiş, fakat mâlen yardım ederek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He contracted adasa, described as a smallpox-like illness, and died from grief seven days after learning Quraysh had been defeated at Badr.
rows.anchor: Kendisi “adese” denilen çiçek kabîlinden bir illete tutulmuş

rows.speaker: Âlûsî
rows.claim: Al-Alusi and others say Quraysh feared adasa like plague; even his family stayed away, and his corpse lay for three days and smelled.
rows.anchor: Âlûsî ve daha sâirlerinin de naklettiği vechile Kureyş adeseden tâun gibi sakındıkları

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One burial account says hired Sudanese carried him, dug a pit, placed him inside with wood, and covered him with stones.
rows.anchor: bir çukur kazıp ağaçlarla içine kakmışlar, örtünceye kadar da üzerine taş atmışlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another burial account says they dug no pit, propped the corpse beside a wall, and threw stones until it was covered.
rows.anchor: diğer bir rivayette çukur da kazmamışlar, bir duvarın dibine dayayıp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The predicted earthly death came about about fifteen years after the revelation, but the verse means enduring bodily and spiritual loss through afterlife punishment too.
rows.anchor: ma‘amâfîh murad, sade böyle oluşundan ibaret değil, dünyada maksadına

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma aghna is either a rhetorical negative question or a direct negation, explaining his ruin: nothing in his wealth saved him or brought good.
rows.anchor: {مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ} bu مَا istifhâm-ı inkârî veya doğrudan doğru nâfiyedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma kasab can be a relative noun or verbal noun, and may likewise be read as a rhetorical question or negation.
rows.anchor: ve kazandığı, yahut kazancı: meksûbâtı veya kesbi bu مَا, mevsul veya masdariyyedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible rendering asks what his wealth and earnings gained him: neither rescued him from disaster nor earned him any good.
rows.anchor: “Ne fâide verdi ona malı? Ve ne kazandı? Onu felâketten kurtaracak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading that neither his property nor his earnings helped him better explains the ruin of both hands.
rows.anchor: lâkin “malı da fâide vermedi ona, kesbi de” mânasına olmak, iki elin hüsrânını

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and earnings may mean capital and its profit, inherited property and self-earned income, or all old and new possessions and gains.
rows.anchor: Malı sermayesi, kesbi de sermayesinden kazandığı kâr, hâsılât ve vâridat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, kasb includes every benefit or effort counted to his account, including children, social standing, customary good works, and his plots against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: evlâdı, mevki‘-i ictimâ‘îsi, itikadınca kendine, kavmine, âdetine iyilik nâmına yaptığı işleri

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets ma kasab as Abu Lahab’s children.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan: “mâkeseb”i veledidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported anecdote says Abu Lahab called his children an evil acquisition after one pushed him while he tried to stop their fight.
rows.anchor: çıkarınız yanımdan bu kesb-i habîsi” demişti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic hadith says a man’s purest food comes from his own earnings and that his child is part of his earnings.
rows.anchor: her adamın yiyeceğinin en temizi kesbindendir, evlâdı da kesbindendir” diye vârid olmuştur

rows.speaker: Dahhâk
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads kasb as Abu Lahab’s evil deed: plotting hostility against the Messenger.
rows.anchor: Dahhâk’ten: “Mâkesebi amel-i habîsi, yani Resûlullah’a adâvette keydidir” diye

rows.speaker: Katâde
rows.claim: Qatada reads kasb as deeds he mistakenly thought good, like the deeds made scattered dust in Furqan 25:23.
rows.anchor: Katâde’den de “mâkesebi, bir iyilik yapıyorum zannıyla yaptığı ameldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abu Lahab claimed he could ransom himself from his nephew’s message with his wealth and children.
rows.anchor: rivayet olunmuştur ki “eğer kardeşimin oğlunun söylediği hak ise ben ondan malımı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These interpretations do not conflict or restrict the meaning: kasb embraces all of them, and neither wealth nor any acquisition saved him.
rows.anchor: Fakat bu mânaların birisi diğerine münâfî değildir, maksad tahsis değil, misâl demektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He will enter an intensely blazing afterlife fire unlike any worldly flame; it burns through souls and reaches hearts, as Humaza 104:6–7 says.
rows.anchor: dünyada misli görülmedik son derece şiddetli bir alev

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is not merely one that burns bodies but the fire that penetrates hearts mentioned in Humaza.
rows.anchor: sade cisimleri yakan bir ateş değil, rûhları sarıp gönüllere muttali‘olan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wife is Umm Jamil, daughter of Harb and sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb; the meanings of these names also carry allusions.
rows.anchor: Karısı da ki Harb’ın kızı Ümmü Cemîl ve Ebû Süfyan b.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife is coordinated with the implicit pronoun referring to Abu Lahab in “he will burn”; she too enters the fire.
rows.anchor: Bu سَيَصْلَىٰ’nın tahtında müstetir Ebû Leheb’e râci‘olan هُوَ zamirine ma‘tuftur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the other readings, hammalatu is nominative as a predicate, making the clause circumstantial rather than coordinated with Abu Lahab.
rows.anchor: Diğer kıraatlerin hepsinde حَمَّالَةَ haber olarak ötre okunur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Asim’s accusative reading, the conjunction permits two grammatical analyses.
rows.anchor: Bizim Âsım kıraatinde ise üstün okunur, vâv atf olur, bunda iki vecih mümkindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first analysis, the accusative is a circumstantial description of the wife: she carries fuel to bring Abu Lahab or intensify his fire, having served his unbelief in life.
rows.anchor: karısı da odun hamalı olarak cehenneme girecek, Ebû Leheb’i götürecek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since disbelievers are the fuel of Hell in Baqara 2:24 and Al Imran 3:10, serving unbelief is like carrying its firewood; Abu Lahab himself may be the wood on her back.
rows.anchor: cehennemin odunu, çırası kâfirler olduğundan küfre hizmet cehenneme odun taşımak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second analysis takes the accusative as blame: “that wood-carrying woman”; a pause after “and his wife” is then permissible, with Abu Lahab himself understood as the wood.
rows.anchor: Zemm üzere mansub olarak, yani “o hammâlete’l-hatab karı” demek olmasıdır

rows.speaker: Keşşâf
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains “carrying wood” figuratively as malicious gossip: one carries kindling between people by stirring up evil.
rows.anchor: Sâhib-Keşşâf der ki: “Nâs arasında nemîmelerle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anonymous poet’s line uses “carrying wet wood” for gossip that spreads greater evil because wet wood produces much smoke.
rows.anchor: Nitekim مِن البِيضِ لم تصْطَدْ عَلَى ظَهْرِ لأَْمَةٍ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turkish idioms such as “kindling” express the gossip sense, but literal “wood carrier” in Turkish conveys humiliation rather than gossip.
rows.anchor: Bu mâna lisânımızda “kundakçılık etmek” tâbiriyle ifade olunur

rows.speaker: İbn Zeyd
rows.claim: The main force is the once-rich, honored woman’s degradation in the afterlife, serving her husband’s torment; considering the other readings, “wood carrier” is clearer.
rows.anchor: biz diğer vecihleri de nazar-ı dikkate alarak “odun hamalı” diye anlatmayı daha vâzıh gördük

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and others report that the wife had thorn branches placed at night on the Prophet’s path to hurt him.
rows.anchor: İbn Zeyd’den ve daha başkalarından rivayet olunmuştur ki: Resûlullah’ın geçeceği yola

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thorn-branch report can also symbolize her covert gossip and other harassment in service of her husband, joining the literal and figurative senses.
rows.anchor: Bu rivayet de onun Peygamber’e ezâ etmek ve dinin neşrine mâni‘olmak için kocasının fikrine hizmet etmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause is circumstantial under the implicit subject of hammala: a rope is on her neck.
rows.anchor: Bu cümle de “hammâle”nin tahtında müstetir هِيَ zamirinden hâldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jid is more specific than ordinary neck: it denotes a fine neck adorned or suited to jewelry, although unuq can also occur in humiliating contexts.
rows.anchor: “Cîd” boyun demek ise de “unuk” gibi sade boyun değil,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the humiliation of “wood carrier,” a rope on an ordinary neck would add no force; jid carries the contrast with a beautiful, ornament-worthy neck.
rows.anchor: burada “odun hamalı” diye tahkirden sonra فيِ عُنُقِهَا حَبْلٌ “boynunda bir ip” denilseydi ziyade bir mâna olmazdı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word jid, also used in praise of a lovely neck, makes a rope replacing jewelry a sharper humiliation; the distinction also exists in Turkish gerdan.
rows.anchor: Hâlbuki “cîd” şâirin وأَحْسَنُ مِنْ جِيدِ الْمَلِيحَةِ حُلِيّها dediği gibi ziynet ve medh ile söylenir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description invokes Zukhruf 43:18: a woman raised amid adornment is demeaned by a porter’s rope, intensifying the passage’s painful irony.
rows.anchor: fehvâsı üzere ziynet ile gerdanlıklarla tezyin ve i‘zâz edilerek yetiştirilen

rows.speaker: Sa‘îd b. Müseyyeb
rows.claim: Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyib and others report that she had a precious jeweled necklace around her neck.
rows.anchor: Fi’l-vâki‘Sa‘îd b. Müseyyeb’den ve sâireden mervîdir ki: Onun gerdanında cevâhirden bir kılâde-i fâhire

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains mesed as a rope made by twisting date-palm fronds into strong fiber; memsuda describes a tightly twisted or braided body.
rows.anchor: Râgıb’ın Müfredât’ında: “‘Mesed’ hurma cerîdinden, yani şahlarından ittihaz edilir de mesd olunur

rows.speaker: Zemahşerî
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says mesed is rope twisted intensely, whether of fiber, leather, or any other material; memsud may mean strongly built.
rows.anchor: Zemahşerî diyor ki: “‘Mesed” iplerden fetl-i şedîd ile fetl edilmiş olandır

rows.speaker: Kâmûs
rows.claim: The Qamus distinguishes mesd, twisting a rope or striving continuously, from mesed, an iron spindle or a rope of palm or muql fiber, also any strong rope.
rows.anchor: Kāmûs’ta mîm’in fethi ve sîn’in sükûnuyla “mesd” ip bükmek

rows.speaker: Besâir
rows.claim: Basa’ir treats mesd as the verbal noun and mesed as a tightly plaited rope, glossing the verse as an iron rope twisted forcefully.
rows.anchor: Besâir’de beyânına göre “mesd” masdar ve fethateynle “mesed” isimdir, memsud mânasınadır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mesed basically means a firm rope twisted or braided from strong fiber, but can describe stout twisted or plaited cord made from hair, leather, iron, or other material.
rows.anchor: Demek ki “mesed” esâsen memsud mânasına olarak hurma veya mukl ağacının lifleri gibi kuvvetli elyaftan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse emphasizes the rope’s strength and suppleness rather than what it is made of, summoning the strongest imaginable cord.
rows.anchor: Burada da murad ipin maddesinden ziyade kuvvetini, kıvraklığını ifade olduğundan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers’ promised restraints include chains in Insan 76:4; for a woman carrying wood, however, a fiber rope tying the load suits the image.
rows.anchor: cehenneme giden kâfirlere mev‘ud olan da zincirler ve bağlardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scene pictures the load-binding rope hanging from her neck where her necklace or braided hair would be, pressing her with humiliation as she carries fuel for the fire.
rows.anchor: Sırtında cehennem odunu olan kocasını taşırken gerek iftihar ettiği gerdanlık ve gerek örgülü kıvrak saçlarının gerdanında sarkışı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image makes a parable of the disgrace awaiting wealth, labor, honor, and lineage not spent in God’s cause or met with gratitude.
rows.anchor: Dünyada Allah yoluna sarfolunmayan o servet ve kesbin, o şükrü bilinmeyen şeref ve hasebin âkıbetindeki hakāretle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening prediction was fulfilled: because Abu Lahab did not believe in God’s oneness, he could not benefit from the Prophet’s intercession; status and wealth did not rescue him.
rows.anchor: Tâ risâletin bidâyetinde haber verilmiş olan bu hakikat böylece tahakkuk etmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He did not repent of saying “tabban lak”; he died in ruin, and the author seeks refuge from an evil ending.
rows.anchor: ona تـَبًّا لَك dediğine tevbe de nasib olmayıp böyle tebâb olmuş gitmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After contrasting the good and ruined endings, the text points to monotheism and sincerity, then refuge in God, as the path to a good end.
rows.anchor: Şimdi biri, tesbih ve hamd ve istiğfar ile Allah’a giden, biri de hüsran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion prepares for Ikhlas by saying that knowing God through pure monotheism and seeking His protection is the remedy for ruin.
rows.anchor: Allah târif edilerek tevhid ve ihlâs ile O’na ilticâ emrolunacaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “Say” addresses the Messenger and, by extension, everyone whose role is to convey the message.
rows.anchor: hitab Resûlullah’a ve dolayısıyla hitab şânından olanların

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit imperative marks this definition as revealed by God and requires it to be stated and conveyed verbatim.
rows.anchor: Emrin tasrîhinde bu târifin bilhassa beyân-ı ilâhî olduğunu ifade ile aynen söylenmesi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawl includes both utterance and meaning: affirm in the heart and state with the tongue that this is God’s revealed word, then convey and advise others to say it in truth.
rows.anchor: Kavil makūle ve melfûza şâmil olur, kemâli de lafız ve mânanın cem‘indedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun huwa has no antecedent within the surah; the revelation’s question points to God, while the preceding Nasr surah may suggest the name Allah.
rows.anchor: sade kendinden bir düşünce ve sırf aklî ve nazarî delillerden bir istidlâl olarak değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the surah is independent and Allah appears again as predicate, huwa’s referent gives meaningful ambiguity amid familiarity, adjusted to the audience.
rows.anchor: Gerek sûrenin istiklâli ve gerek lisânî

rows.speaker: İbn Sînâ
rows.claim: Ibn Sina takes huwa to refer to God’s essence: at the level of essence, nothing but “He” can define what intellects cannot grasp.
rows.anchor: İbn Sînâ bu sûrenin tefsîrinde bu zamir Allah teâlâ’nın mertebe-i zâtında

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the three words indicate three stages of seekers; the highest, the mukarrabun, see no true existent but God because only He is necessary in Himself.
rows.anchor: Fahr-ı Râzî de demiştir ki: “Burada هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ üç lafız vardır

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: For the mukarrabun, all else is contingent and therefore nonexistent when considered in itself; the absolute pointer huwa suffices when its referent is fixed as God.
rows.anchor: Bunlar ki eşyânın min haysü hiye hiye mâhiyyât

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: On these readings huwa refers to God’s essence rather than merely His name; it may be better treated as a divine name, since pronouns can receive attributes as in Baqara 2:163.
rows.anchor: Lizâtihi mümkin olan da min haysü hüve hüve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether construed as a pronoun or name, huwa is the subject, Allah its predicate, and ahad a second predicate: “He is Allah, one.”
rows.anchor: Nitekim zamir tavsif olunmadığı hâlde وَإِلَٰهُكُمْ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ’de [el-Bakara 2/163]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For those who see only the necessary Being as truly existent, saying “He” identifies God, whose existence and necessary being cannot be absent even for an instant.
rows.anchor: vücûdunu muktezî ve bir an için bile yokluğunu farz ve tasavvur etmek mümteni‘

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s second stage, the people of the right, recognizes both God and created beings; plurality requires the name Allah to distinguish the Creator from creation.
rows.anchor: Bunlar Hakk’ı mevcud tanırlar, halkı da mevcud tanırlar

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: For this stage, Allah names the self-sufficient Being who gathers all perfection and alone deserves divinity.
rows.anchor: Allah, mâ‘adâsı kendiye muhtaç, kendisi mâ‘adânın hepsinden müstağnî bütün sıfât-ı kemâli câmi‘

rows.speaker: Fahr-ı Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s lowest stage, the people of the left, allow multiple gods; ahad explicitly refutes their view.
rows.anchor: Bunlar vâcibu’l-vücudun, ilâhın birden ziyade olmasını tecviz ederler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another, more famous and rhetorically clearer analysis makes huwa the pronoun of the matter: an initially ambiguous subject announces a significant statement.
rows.anchor: Bu “Hüve” zamirinde diğer bir vecih de zamîr-i şân olmaktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the pronoun-of-the-matter analysis, “Allah is One” explains the important proposition announced by huwa; Allah is the subject and ahad its predicate.
rows.anchor: Bu surette haberi ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ cümlesi olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposition is that God, possessing all majesty and beauty, alone has divinity and is the one with no partner, as Shura 42:11 teaches.
rows.anchor: لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِۦ شَىْءٌۭ [eş-Şûrâ 42/11] hep bir, yegâne birdir

rows.speaker: Nihâye
rows.claim: Nihaya defines ahad as the unique One who was and remains alone, with no other alongside Him; the name negates any number in addition.
rows.anchor: Nihâye’de: “Allah teâlâ’nın esmâsında Ehad هُوَ الْفَرْدُ الَّذِي لَمْ يـَزَلْ وَحْدَهُ

rows.speaker: Nihâye
rows.claim: Nihaya illustrates ahad’s number-denying use with “no one came to me” and says its hamza replaces an original waw from wahd.
rows.anchor: مَا جَاءَنِي أَحَدٌ ‘bana hiçbir ehad gelmedi’ dersin, bunda hemze vâv’dan bedeldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahad can mean wahid, “one,” but is stronger in the core sense of excluding anything else: a real unity that can never be two.
rows.anchor: “Ehad” lafzı bir demek olan “vâhid” mânasında dahi kullanılır ise de aralarında mühim farklar vardır

rows.speaker: Ezherî
rows.claim: Al-Azhari, as quoted by al-Razi, says only God may be described as ahad; one cannot say “one man” or “one dirham” with ahad, though wahid allows it.
rows.anchor: Râzî’nin naklettiği vechile Ezherî demiştir ki: “‘Ehadiyet’ ile Allah teâlâ’dan başka bir şey tavsif olunmaz

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari distinguishes them because every ahad is wahid, but not every wahid is ahad.
rows.anchor: Birincisi ‘vâhid’ ‘ehad’de dâhil olur, ‘ehad’ ‘vâhid’de dâhil olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “no one can withstand him” with wahid could allow two opponents, but with ahad it excludes any number of opponents.
rows.anchor: denildiği zaman ‘bir mukāvemet edemez’ demek olduğundan ‘lâkin iki mukāvemet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wahid is normally used affirmatively, while ahad is used in negation with universal force: “I saw one man” versus “I saw no one.”
rows.anchor: Üçüncüsü ‘vâhid’ isbatta, ‘ehad’ nefyde kullanılır

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says negative ahad ranges over all speaking beings, singly or together and in any number, as in “there is no one in the house.”
rows.anchor: Râgıb der ki: “‘Ehad’ iki suretle isti‘mâl olunur: Birisi yalnız nefyde birisi de isbatta

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: This exhaustive negative use cannot be used affirmatively, since that would assert both one individual and the numbers above one.
rows.anchor: Bu mâna için isbatta isti‘mâli sahih olmaz

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Al-Raghib lists three affirmative uses: in eleven and twenty-one, in an annexed phrase meaning “first,” and as a description reserved for God in this verse.
rows.anchor: İsbatta müsta‘mel olan ‘ehad’e gelince: O da üç vechiledir

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: The annexed use meaning “first” appears in Yusuf 12:41 and in the name of Sunday; affirmative ahad as an adjective is unique to God.
rows.anchor: أَمَّآ أَحَدُكُمَا فَيَسْقِى رَبَّهُۥ خَمْرًۭا [Yûsuf 12/41] kavl-i kerîmi gibi ve يـَوْمُ الأَْحَدِ dedikleri gibi

rows.speaker: Râgıb
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says the affirmative ahad derives from wahad, which can describe others, as shown by al-Nabigha’s verse.
rows.anchor: velâkin ‘vehad’ gayrısında kullanılır. Nitekim Nâbiga

rows.speaker: Ebussuud
rows.claim: Abu al-Su‘ud and others say the hamza replacing waw occurs in affirmative ahad, as in Jinn 72:18 and Ikhlas 112:4; universal negative ahad has original hamza.
rows.anchor: Ebussuud ve daha başkalarının beyânına göre hemzesi vâv’dan mübdel olan “ehad” isbattakidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some also say both hamzas are original; in this surah both forms occur.
rows.anchor: Bu sûrede ikisi de zikredilmiştir

rows.speaker: Sa‘leb
rows.claim: Tha‘lab says ahad does not begin a counting sequence or qualify a man, whereas wahid does; al-Khalil reportedly allowed ahad wa-ithnan meaning one and two.
rows.anchor: Sa‘leb şöyle fark etmiştir: “‘Ehad’

rows.speaker: Hanefiyyeden bazıları
rows.claim: Some Hanafis distinguish ahadiyya as never accepting parts or number, whereas wahidiyya can accept both, as in “one hundred” or “one thousand.”
rows.anchor: Hanefiyyeden bazıları da farkı şöyle nakleylemiştir: Ehadiyet hiçbir hâlde cüz’iyete ve adediyete muhtemil olmaz

rows.speaker: Hattâbî
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi says ahadiyya denies partners in essence while wahidiyya denies shared attributes; other theologians give the reverse account, denying any partner in essence or attributes.
rows.anchor: Hattâbî “ehadiyet zâtın teferrüdü, vâhidiyet sıfatta

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas ve Ebû Ubeyde
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to gloss ahad as wahid, defined as that which accepts no division or composition.
rows.anchor: Nitekim İbn Abbas’ın ve Ebû Ubeyde’nin de bunu “vâhid” diye tefsir ettikleri söylenmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Glossing ahad as wahid is easiest for readers, but this must not erase the distinction: ahad includes wahid, while ahad is the fuller unity.
rows.anchor: Allah teâlâ hakkında “vâhid” ve “ehad” birbirinden ayrılmamak itibariyle ikisi de birdir

rows.speaker: Ebu’l-Bekā
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa says ahad can also mean wahid, while preserving distinctions between the terms.
rows.anchor: Ebu’l-Bekā, Külliyyât’ında “ehad”ın “vâhid” mânasına da geldiğini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that wahid denies numerical plurality but can still allow relative plurality, so ahad is preferred for transcendence.
rows.anchor: vâhidiyet adedî ta‘addüdün intifâsından ibarettir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wahid can describe unity at different levels, while ahad is its most perfect degree; where the term is open-ended, it denotes the highest possible unity.
rows.anchor: “Vâhid” muhtelif merâtibde birliklere söylenebilir, “ehad” ise onun ekmelidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity is coextensive with existence in predication, not identical in meaning: every unity exists and every existent has unity, including a multitude such as ten.
rows.anchor: yani mefhumda değil hamlde müsâvî olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity and multiplicity oppose each other only under different aspects; dividing a body removes its unity but not its existence.
rows.anchor: Bir cismi parçalamak birliğini yok etmek olsa da varlığını yok etmek olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity is not existence or essence itself; it is an additional concept upon an essence, which can admit unity or plurality, and unity precedes plurality.
rows.anchor: Onun için mâhiyet vahdeti de kesreti de kābil olur. Ve vahdet, kesretten evveldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity is the state of not being divisible into things sharing the same reality; multiplicity is divisibility into such things, whether division is into individuals or parts.
rows.anchor: Şeyin hakikatte kendisine müşareket eder umûrda inkısam etmez olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is better to define unity and multiplicity simply by indivisibility and divisibility, since division into individuals or parts is secondary detail.
rows.anchor: kesret inkısam eder olması haysiyeti demek daha iyidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity has degrees, and a thing’s being one may be essential or accidental; being one contrasts with many only accidentally.
rows.anchor: ‘vâhid’ denilen şeyin vahdetle ittisâfı da zâtî ve arazî

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Something may be one in one respect and many in another, but it cannot be both in the same respect.
rows.anchor: bir şey bir cihetten vâhid iken diğer cihetten veya cihetlerden kesîr olabilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An individual one cannot be applied to multiple particulars; a non-individual one can be divided among particulars because its concept permits shared instances.
rows.anchor: tasavvuru çoğa hamledilmesine mâni‘olursa o, şahsî vâhiddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true individual one accepts no division at all; if indivisibility is its only meaning it is unity itself, otherwise it has another meaning, with or without position.
rows.anchor: şahsî vâhid, eğer hiç inkısam kabul etmezse, yani cüz’îlere münkasim olmadığı gibi cüzlere de ayrılmazsa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A true one with position is a point; one without position is an abstract being grasped by intellect, like the sense of “I,” “you,” or “he.”
rows.anchor: Eğer bir vaz‘ı varsa, yani işâret-i hissiyeyi kābil ise o noktadır, vaz‘ı yoksa o müfârıktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An individual that cannot divide into particulars but has parts in quantity is continuously one when its parts resemble each other, like a simple body, and collectively one when unlike, like a tree.
rows.anchor: Müşâbih ise o bi’l-ittisâl vâhiddir, cism-i basît gibi; yok eğer muhtelif ise o da bi’l-ictimâ‘vâhiddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A non-individual one is one in one respect and many in another; its unity is essential when part of the multiplicity’s essence, otherwise accidental.
rows.anchor: Gayr-i şahsî vâhide gelince, ki o bir cihetten vâhid diğer cihetten kesîrdir, onun vahdeti ciheti ya zâtîsidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Essential unity may be the whole essence, making one by species, or an essential part, making unity by genus when common or by specific difference when not.
rows.anchor: Eğer zâtî ise o zâtî ya mâhiyetinin tamamıdır, bu nev‘an vâhiddir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accidental unity can be by a shared subject, as laughing and crying belong to humanity, or a shared predicate, as cotton and snow are white.
rows.anchor: ‘gülen ile ağlayan insanlıkta birdir’ gibi veya mahmul olur, ‘pamuk ve kar beyazlıkta birdir’ gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the unity is neither essential nor accidental and is not a predicate, it is relational, as the soul’s relation to the body resembles a king’s relation to a city.
rows.anchor: ‘nefsin bedene nisbeti melikin medineye nisbetidir’ denilmesi böyledir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One is predicated analogically rather than equally: an individual one outranks kinds such as species, genus, and difference; essential unity outranks accidental unity, which outranks relational unity.
rows.anchor: şahsî vâhid nev‘iyle vâhidden evlâ, o cinsiyle vâhidden evlâ, o faslıyla vâhidden evlâ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among individual ones, a true indivisible one is more properly one than something that permits any kind of division.
rows.anchor: hiç inkısam kabul etmeyen hakīkī vâhid, bivechin-mâ inkısam kabul edenden evlâdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Things called one differ in reality; distinct beings share the concepts of existence and unity only accidentally, so sharing “one” does not entail sharing every property.
rows.anchor: Vücûdât-ı hâssa hakikatleri muhtelif olmakla beraber

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unity may be existential, conceptual, added to an essence, identical with an essence, or part of an essence; other attributes vary similarly.
rows.anchor: Vücûdîsi de vardır, itibârîsi de vardır, mâhiyet üzere zâid olanı da vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names for non-individual unities include resemblance by species, likeness by genus, similarity in quality, equality in quantity, similarity in shape, alignment in position, correspondence at the ends, and relation.
rows.anchor: Nevide olan vahdete ‘mümaselet’, cinste ‘mücaneset’, keyfiyette ‘müşabehet’, kemmiyette ‘müsâvat’
